messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 54, Mark Jensen had spent most of his adult life in the woods. As a forester, he was used to reading terrain, judging distances, and making decisions that affected other people’s safety. Before the accident, that competence had been central to how he understood himself: steady, practical, the one others trusted. He was married and had built his life around work that required calm attention and confidence in his own judgment. The event that brought him into treatment shattered that sense of himself in a way he still described as almost unbelievable.

The accident happened during a workday in close quarters with another man. Mark had been engaged in routine forestry work when a decision he made resulted in another person being seriously injured. He returned again and again to the physical arrangement of the moment: how close they were standing, where his own body had been positioned, how quickly the injury happened once things went wrong. In recounting it, he did not speak in broad summary. He would suddenly stiffen in his chair and hold his body as though he were back there, braced in the same posture he had been in at the instant of the accident. What came back to him was not only an image but a bodily reliving of position and tension, as if his muscles still knew the exact stance of that moment.

In the days after, he found himself seized by memories of the injured man’s face and body. Reminders of the victim were especially potent. If he caught sight of someone built similarly, moving in a similar way, or if anything specifically called that man to mind, Mark felt his stomach drop. Physical proximity became difficult in a way that had not been true before. If someone came too near him, especially unexpectedly, he felt a jolt of alarm and a powerful urge to shift away. Around strangers this was worse. Even in ordinary situations, a person approaching him could feel dangerous, and he would watch closely for any sign of possible harm. He knew on some level that he might be standing in a safe place, but he could not relax into that knowledge. His body remained tight and ready, scanning other people rather than settling.

Physical pain also became a trigger. Pain in part of his body could abruptly pull him back to the accident, as though the sensation opened a door to the memory. When that happened, the recollection came with intense emotion. Sometimes what surged up first was rage—raw, immediate, and hard for him to understand, because it appeared alongside overwhelming grief. He spoke of being furious when the memory hit, then almost in the same breath overcome by sorrow about what had happened to the other man and what had been taken from both of them. These reactions did not feel chosen. They arrived with force, leaving him feeling shaken and ashamed afterward.

Over the following months, Mark’s confidence in himself eroded. He had come to believe there was something about him that made the event happen, as if the accident exposed a defect in his character rather than a terrible outcome of a single moment. He no longer trusted his own judgment. Tasks that had once felt automatic now seemed loaded with the possibility that he would make another catastrophic mistake. At work, this was especially painful. Forestry had defined him, but in the same forests that had once felt familiar, he now felt fundamentally altered. Being near coworkers in the field could make him acutely aware of distance, bodies, and risk. He monitored where people stood and how they moved, and when anyone came near him unexpectedly he would tense and pull back. The work setting that used to confirm who he was now confronted him with the conviction that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had always defined him.

At home, his wife saw the cost even when he tried not to speak about it. Mark was more guarded, less able to settle in his own house, and increasingly preoccupied by the sense that he could not rely on himself. He did not describe this as simple guilt. It felt larger and more final: proof, to him, that he was not the man he had thought he was. What frightened him most was not only remembering the accident, but the possibility that the accident had revealed something permanent—that he was unsafe to trust, unsafe to stand close to, no longer fit for the work and identity he had built his life around.

By the time he sought help, the strain of living this way had become too difficult to contain. He was exhausted by staying on guard around other people and by the way memories overtook both his body and emotions. He came in wanting some way to be near others without bracing, to be in his own body without being thrown back into that moment, and to know whether there was any path to living as himself again. What he feared most was that there was not—that the accident had permanently stripped him of the steadiness and competence he once counted on.
